title: EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF & Deletion Receipts
summary: Map the EU AI Act, as amended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus, and the voluntary NIST AI RMF to engineering artifacts -- risk tiers, log retention, decommissioning -- then design signed deletion receipts as an evidence practice, kept clearly separate from what any regulation requires.
objectives: State the EU AI Act's application dates as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, and identify which article governs a system in the prohibited, high-risk, or transparency tier.
Reconcile the AI Act's log-retention floor (Articles 12, 19, 26(6)) with GDPR storage limitation and the right to erasure in one retention design.
Use the NIST AI RMF functions and the Generative AI Profile's decommissioning and deletion-tracking actions as an operating model, recognising the framework is voluntary.
Design a signed deletion receipt modelled on NIST's certificate of sanitization, and label precisely which of its fields answer a legal obligation and which are engineering practice.

sections.title: What the EU AI Act says, and when, after the Digital Omnibus
paragraphs: This module explains regulatory text for engineers. It is not legal advice, and whether a particular system falls into a given category is a legal determination this module does not make. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act, sets its timing in Article 113: it entered into force on the twentieth day after publication in the Official Journal and applies from 2 August 2026, with exceptions. As adopted, Chapters I and II applied from 2 February 2025; Chapter III Section 4, Chapter V, Chapter VII, Chapter XII, and Article 78 from 2 August 2025 (except Article 101); and Article 6(1) with its corresponding obligations from 2 August 2027.

Those dates have since changed. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026 -- the Digital Omnibus on AI, published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and in force from the third day after publication -- rewrote parts of Article 113's third paragraph. Chapter III Sections 1, 2, and 3 (the high-risk classification rules, requirements, and provider and deployer obligations), except Article 6(5), now apply from 2 December 2027 for systems classified high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III, and from 2 August 2028 for systems classified under Article 6(1) and Annex I. Chapters I and II keep 2 February 2025, except the new prohibitions in Article 5(1), points (ba) and (bb), and Article 5(1a) and (1b), which apply from 2 December 2026; a new point (d) applies Articles 102 to 110 from 27 July 2026. Point (b), covering Chapter V and the other 2 August 2025 provisions, was not amended. The Omnibus's recitals give the reason for the high-risk delay: standards, common specifications, guidance, and national competent authorities were not ready in time.

The tiers each have a governing article. Article 5 lists prohibited practices; the Omnibus added (ba), AI systems that generate or manipulate realistic images, video, audio, or similar material depicting an identifiable person's intimate parts or sexually explicit activity without that person's explicit consent, and (bb), systems that generate or manipulate material or performances within the meaning of Article 2, points (c) and (e), of Directive 2011/93/EU on combating the sexual abuse and sexual exploitation of children. Breaching Article 5 carries fines under Article 99(3) of up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. Article 6 defines high-risk: under 6(1), safety components of products covered by the Union legislation in Annex I that require third-party conformity assessment; under 6(2), the use cases in Annex III. Article 6(3) lets an Annex III system escape the high-risk label if it poses no significant risk -- for example, it performs a narrow procedural task or a preparatory task -- but a system that profiles natural persons is always high-risk, and under 6(4) a provider relying on the derogation must document that assessment before placing the system on the market.

Annex III point 3 deserves attention from anyone building learning technology. It lists AI systems intended to determine access or admission to educational and vocational training institutions, to evaluate learning outcomes -- including when those outcomes are used to steer the learning process -- in such institutions at all levels, to assess the level of education a person will receive or can access, and to monitor prohibited behaviour during tests. Separately, Article 50 sets transparency duties that do not depend on the high-risk tier: 50(1) requires that people be informed they are interacting with an AI system unless that is obvious, and 50(2) requires providers of systems generating synthetic audio, image, video, or text to mark outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format. The Omnibus added Article 111(4): generative systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 must comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026.
sections.callout: Cite Article 113 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. A compliance plan written against the 2024 text alone still shows high-risk obligations starting on 2 August 2026.

sections.title: Logs are required, and so is forgetting
paragraphs: Article 12(1) requires high-risk AI systems to technically allow the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system. Article 12(2) says what the logging is for: identifying situations that may present a risk or a substantial modification, facilitating post-market monitoring under Article 72, and monitoring operation as Article 26(5) requires of deployers. For remote biometric identification systems in Annex III point 1(a), Article 12(3) sets a minimum field list, including the start and end of each use and the reference database checked.

Retention has a floor. Article 19(1) requires providers to keep the automatically generated logs under their control for a period appropriate to the system's intended purpose, of at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law -- in particular Union law on the protection of personal data -- provides otherwise. Article 26(6) places the same duty on deployers. Article 12 sits in Chapter III Section 2 and Articles 19 and 26 in Section 3, so under amended Article 113 these duties apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems -- building the logging now is cheaper than retrofitting it. Non-compliance with deployer obligations under Article 26 is among the infringements Article 99(4) fines at up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

GDPR pulls the other way. Article 5(1)(c) requires personal data to be limited to what is necessary (data minimisation), and Article 5(1)(e) requires it to be kept in identifiable form no longer than necessary (storage limitation). Article 17(1) gives data subjects the right to erasure without undue delay on stated grounds, among them that the data are no longer necessary, consent is withdrawn, or the processing was unlawful; Article 17(3) lists exceptions, including processing necessary for compliance with a legal obligation and for legal claims. Article 12(3) requires the controller to tell the data subject what action was taken within one month of the request, extendable by two further months where necessary, and Article 19 requires the controller to communicate any erasure to each recipient to whom the data were disclosed, unless that proves impossible or involves disproportionate effort.

The Omnibus adds a deletion rule inside the AI Act itself. The new Article 4a lets providers exceptionally process special categories of personal data where strictly necessary for bias detection and correction in high-risk systems, under conditions that include documented access controls and, in 4a(1)(e), deletion once the bias has been corrected or the data reach the end of their retention period, whichever comes first. The engineering consequence of all of this is one design, not two: a log store needs a stated retention period tied to its purpose, personal data in logs kept to what that purpose needs, and a way to find which records concern which person. Whether a retention duty displaces a particular erasure request is a legal question; making both answerable is an engineering one.

sections.title: The NIST AI RMF as an operating model
paragraphs: NIST released the AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0, NIST AI 100-1) on 26 January 2023, and states that it is intended for voluntary use. NIST's framework page also notes that AI RMF 1.0 is being revised as part of the White House AI Action Plan. Nothing in it is a legal requirement; its value here is as an operating model that turns obligations like those above into owned, repeatable work.

The Core has four functions: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE. GOVERN is cross-cutting and applies to all stages of an organisation's AI risk management; MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE apply in system-specific contexts and at specific lifecycle stages. The framework says its actions are not a checklist or an ordered set of steps, that organisations may select among categories and subcategories, and that after establishing GOVERN most users start with MAP.

Several subcategories map directly onto the artifacts this module builds. GOVERN 1.1: legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood, managed, and documented -- the amended Article 113 timeline lives here. GOVERN 1.6: mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems. GOVERN 1.7: processes exist for decommissioning and phasing out AI systems safely. MANAGE 2.4: mechanisms exist to supersede, disengage, or deactivate systems whose performance or outcomes are inconsistent with intended use. MANAGE 4.1: post-deployment monitoring plans include input capture, appeal and override, decommissioning, incident response, recovery, and change management.

The Generative AI Profile, NIST AI 600-1 (26 July 2024), adds suggested actions for generative systems across twelve risks, including Data Privacy, Information Security, and Value Chain and Component Integration. Under GOVERN 1.7, GV-1.7-002 asks organisations to consider, when decommissioning generative systems, data retention requirements, data security, data leakage after decommissioning, and dependencies between upstream and downstream systems. Under MANAGE 4.1, MG-4.1-006 suggests tracking dataset modifications for provenance by monitoring data deletions, rectification requests, and other changes that may affect the verifiability of content origins. GV-1.5-003 suggests a document retention policy that keeps the history of testing, evaluation, validation, and verification. Together they describe a deletion practice that leaves evidence -- which is where receipts come in.

sections.title: Deletion receipts: an engineering practice, not a legal mandate
paragraphs: Be exact about what the law asks for. None of the texts read for this module -- AI Act Articles 4a, 12, 19, and 26, and GDPR Articles 5, 12, 17, and 19 -- prescribes a cryptographic deletion receipt. What they require is erasure on the stated grounds (GDPR Article 17, AI Act Article 4a(1)(e) for bias-correction data), communicating erasure to recipients (GDPR Article 19), telling the data subject what action was taken within the deadline (GDPR Article 12(3)), and being responsible for, and able to demonstrate, compliance with the processing principles (GDPR Article 5(2)). A signed receipt is one way an engineering team can make that demonstration verifiable. It is a design choice, and it should be described internally as one.

The closest published precedent is NIST SP 800-88 Revision 2, Guidelines for Media Sanitization (September 2025). Its section 4.6 says a certificate of sanitization should be completed for each piece of sanitized media and may be a physical or an electronic record. It lists what the certificate records, including the sanitization method (clear, purge, or destroy), the technique, the tool used including its version, the verification method, and the name, title, date, location, contact information, and signature of the people performing verification and validation. SP 800-88 governs storage media, not individual database records; adapting the certificate's shape to per-record deletion is this module's extrapolation, not NIST guidance.

Signing makes the receipt tamper-evident. FIPS 186-5, the Digital Signature Standard, states that digital signatures detect unauthorized modifications to data and authenticate the identity of the signatory, and that a recipient can use a signature to show a third party it was generated by the claimed signatory -- non-repudiation. It approves three techniques: RSA, ECDSA, and EdDSA. A workable receipt signs a canonical serialisation of fields such as: a request reference; a keyed or salted reference to the data subject rather than raw identifiers; the grounds; each store the data reached -- primary database, search or vector index, caches, analytics, backups, logs, evaluation datasets -- with its state (deleted, scheduled with a date, or retained with a stated basis); the verification method for each store; the tool and version; recipients notified; and timestamps.

A receipt is a claim, and it is only as true as what stands behind it. SP 800-88r2 notes that when lifecycle tracking breaks down, sanitization records show only that specific media were sanitized, not whether all media were -- the per-record equivalent is that a receipt proves deletion from the stores you listed, not from the ones you forgot, which is why the data inventory matters as much as the signature. A receipt that contains the deleted personal data defeats its own purpose. For backups, SP 800-88r2 describes cryptographic erase as sanitizing the keys that encrypt the data, and it attaches conditions: all copies of the target keys must be able to be sanitized, CE cannot sanitize sensitive data that was previously stored on the media in plaintext, and CE should not be trusted on backed-up or escrowed media without high confidence in how the keys were managed. Per-subject key destruction for backups borrows that idea; if you use it, carry those conditions into the design and mark backups 'scheduled' until the keys and copies are verifiably gone.

Receipt issuance records the current handling of a request; it does not establish completion of all deletion obligations. Here backups are still scheduled, so overall deletion remains pending and deletionCompletedAt is null. Track each pending store to verified completion, preserve the basis and review record for any lawful retention, and issue a new signed status receipt. A signature authenticates the statement, not the truth or completeness of the deletion evidence.

sections.title: Worked case: a scoped deletion request with retained records
paragraphs: Case boundary: an AI-assisted feedback feature processes the synthetic reference `synthetic-subj-042`. No actual personal data is present, no storage is contacted, and no live deletion occurs. The supplied expected inventory contains seven stores: a primary store, cache, vector index, logs, backup, evaluation dataset, and downstream recipient.

The initial response records `requestHandlingStatus: complete` because the request has been received, scoped, and answered. Its `receiptStatus` remains `pending` because four stores have unresolved dispositions. Receipt issuance, request handling, and scoped deletion completion are separate facts. A scheduled date passing is not evidence that deletion occurred.

The later update records verified deletion for the primary store, cache, vector index, backup, evaluation dataset, and downstream recipient. Logs remain retained under a documented scope, basis, and review date after the synthetic legal-review decision is marked complete. Therefore `deletionCompletedAt` means completion of the documented request-scoped disposition. It does not mean that every physical copy has disappeared.

The receipt cannot establish the disposition of an omitted store, an undisclosed model-training copy, an unknown provider backup, a prior plaintext copy, or data outside the recipient attestation. Those matters remain UNKNOWN unless inventory, lineage, contract, key-management, and recipient evidence establish them. The protocol is provider-neutral and makes no deletion guarantee about Meta, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Phi, Z.ai, OpenAI, or any other provider.
sections.callout: A signature authenticates and protects the integrity of a statement. It does not establish that the inventory is complete or that the underlying deletion occurred. This lab labels its signature envelope unexecuted and does not substitute SHA-256 or HMAC for a FIPS 186-5 asymmetric signature. See https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.186-5.pdf and https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-88r2.pdf

sections.title: Completed retention map for the synthetic feature
paragraphs: The periods below are supplied engineering-policy inputs, not new legal conclusions. UNKNOWN is used where the supplied facts do not establish a period or capability. Open questions stay open until the identified review or evidence is obtained.

Store: primary-feedback-db. Data held: Subject reference, submission reference, generated feedback. Retention period: Proposed 30 days after request. Purpose: Serve feedback and support request handling. Driver or boundary: Storage limitation; any appeal exception is UNKNOWN pending review. Initial disposition and evidence: Deleted with verified synthetic lookup evidence.

Store: response-cache. Data held: Prompt and response cache entry. Retention period: Proposed 24 hours. Purpose: Reduce duplicate processing. Driver or boundary: Engineering minimisation choice; no separate legal retention basis supplied. Initial disposition and evidence: Deleted with verified synthetic cache-miss evidence.

Store: submission-vector-index. Data held: Embedding and document identifier. Retention period: Proposed 30 days. Purpose: Similarity retrieval. Driver or boundary: Whether a particular embedding is personal data is a legal-review boundary. Initial disposition and evidence: Deleted with verified synthetic index-query evidence.

Store: grading-event-logs. Data held: Event metadata, subject reference, timestamps, operation result. Retention period: Proposed six months if the relevant logging duties apply; final legal basis is case-dependent. Purpose: Safety monitoring, incident review, accountability. Driver or boundary: AI Act Articles 12, 19, and 26(6), GDPR storage limitation, and system classification require scoped review. Initial disposition and evidence: Retained; legal review initially incomplete.

Store: nightly-backups. Data held: Encrypted backup copies. Retention period: Proposed 35-day rotation; exact key-copy coverage UNKNOWN until verified. Purpose: Disaster recovery. Driver or boundary: Rotation, prior plaintext, escrowed keys, and all key copies require evidence. Initial disposition and evidence: Scheduled initially.

Store: evaluation-dataset. Data held: Submission-derived example, feedback label, evaluation metadata. Retention period: UNKNOWN. Purpose: Regression evaluation. Driver or boundary: Provenance, effective de-identification, and permitted retention need review. Initial disposition and evidence: Scheduled initially.

Store: downstream-feedback-processor. Data held: Submission and generated feedback disclosed for processing. Retention period: UNKNOWN until contract and recipient evidence are checked. Purpose: Generate or post-process feedback. Driver or boundary: Recipient custody, backups, training use, and deletion capability are UNKNOWN. Initial disposition and evidence: Request acknowledged; deletion unverified.

The initial log record has a proposed operational basis, a scope label, and a review date, but legalReviewComplete is false. That unresolved review prevents scoped completion. The later fixture changes the legal-review state only after a synthetic verified review record is supplied. The retained record is not described as erased.

Inventory completeness is tested independently. The validator compares every receipt to expected_inventory.json; it does not accept inventoryComplete: true as proof by itself. Empty, missing, extra, or duplicate store lists cannot support completion.
sections.callout: NIST AI RMF GOVERN 1.6 addresses inventory and GOVERN 1.7 addresses decommissioning. NIST AI 600-1 GV-1.7-002 and MG-4.1-006 address retention during decommissioning and deletion tracking. These frameworks are voluntary operating guidance: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf and https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf

sections.title: Receipt fields, evidence rules, and supported claims
paragraphs: The validator accepts only the store states `deleted`, `scheduled`, and `retained`; only JSON booleans for boolean fields; and timezone-aware ISO-8601 timestamps. `deleted` requires a resolved, verified deletion record. `scheduled` requires a future `until` timestamp relative to receipt issuance and a resolved pending scheduling record. `retained` requires a basis, a narrow `scopeLabel`, a review or expiry timestamp, a boolean legal-review result, and matching evidence.

Each `evidenceRefs` value must resolve in the independently supplied registry. The evidence record must name the same store and a compatible action. A deleted store cannot cite contradictory pending evidence. Every verified disposition used for completion must occur no earlier than the request and no later than `deletionCompletedAt`. Completion itself must satisfy `requestReceived <= deletionCompletedAt <= receiptIssuedAt`. A completion timestamp before receipt issuance is valid when the evidence supports that chronology.

`receiptStatus` records whether the request-scoped disposition is pending or complete. `requestHandlingStatus` separately records handling of the request and may be complete while deletion is pending. `completionScope` must be `request-scoped-disposition`; the validator does not support an all-physical-copies claim. Future completion or verification timestamps are rejected relative to receipt issuance.

Field support is traceable as follows: `requestReceived` and `requestHandlingStatus` support documenting the response process; `stores`, `evidenceRefs`, `inventoryComplete`, `completionScope`, and the strict state machine are engineering controls; recipient evidence supports the underlying recipient-notification workflow; `deletionCompletedAt` is an engineering record of scoped completion; and `signature` is an unexecuted illustration of an engineering authenticity envelope. No regulation cited in the lesson prescribes this receipt format.

NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 describes certificate and verification records for media sanitization, not proof of per-record deletion. Its cryptographic-erase limits matter here: all relevant key copies must be sanitizable, and destroying keys does not cure data previously stored in plaintext. See https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-88r2.pdf.

Worked case: the evidence envelope has subjectRef "synthetic-subj-042" and requestReceived "2026-09-02T14:05:00Z". A receipt with the same subjectRef and requestReceived is scope-compatible. For a retained store, reviewAt "2027-03-02T00:00:00Z" is valid for the supplied fixtures because it is after receiptIssuedAt, and all supplied fixture reviewAt values are 2027-03-02. The freshness decision is deliberately made against receiptIssuedAt, not requestReceived: a review at 2026-09-02T14:09:00Z would be after the request but invalid if receiptIssuedAt is 2026-09-02T14:10:00Z. This prevents a review from being treated as fresh merely because it followed the request. An independent changed-input task is to change only receipt.subjectRef to "synthetic-subj-999" while leaving the envelope unchanged. The traceable expected decision is invalid, with the subject mismatch error. A second negative fixture changes only requestReceived to "2026-09-02T14:06:00Z"; the expected decision is invalid, with the requestReceived mismatch error. These are expected results derived from the inputs, not claimed execution results.

The envelope binds evidence scope but is not cryptographic authority. A signature does not prove that erasures occurred; deletion evidence must still be evaluated by the validator and its recorded statuses.
sections.callout: The validator checks record consistency against supplied synthetic fixtures. It cannot authenticate evidence, verify an asymmetric signature, inspect backups, detect forgotten stores, determine whether an embedding is personal data, or establish what a vendor did.

sections.title: File 3: validator.py
paragraphs: Save this as `validator.py`. It uses only the Python standard library. It validates structure, strict types, expected inventory coverage, evidence resolution, chronology, state consistency, request handling, and completion claims. It performs no deletion, network access, provider call, cryptographic signing, or signature verification.
sections.callout: The output is deterministic compact JSON. A valid record exits with status 0. An invalid record exits with status 1 and includes actionable errors.

sections.title: File 7: negative_cases.py
paragraphs: Save this as `negative_cases.py`. It constructs meaningful failures without modifying the fixtures on disk. The tests cover empty, missing, extra, and duplicate stores; malformed store, state, signature algorithm, and receipt status types; a forged completion claim; a stale schedule; and an externally controlled store represented as deleted using only pending acknowledgement evidence.

The test harness asserts both rejection and useful diagnostic text. A Python exception or an unexpected acceptance causes the script to fail. This demonstrates controlled validation for values such as `store: []`, `state: {}`, and `signature.alg: []` before membership or set operations.

import json
from validator import validate


def load(path):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        return json.load(handle)


inventory = load("expected_inventory.json")
evidence = load("evidence_registry.json")
initial = load("initial.json")
later = load("later.json")

cases = []

value = copy.deepcopy(later)
value["stores"] = []
cases.append(("empty-stores", value, "stores: expected non-empty array"))

value = copy.deepcopy(later)
value["stores"] = [item for item in value["stores"] if item["store"] != "nightly-backups"]
cases.append(("missing-backup", value, "inventory: missing stores: nightly-backups"))

value = copy.deepcopy(later)
value["stores"].append({"store":"shadow-copy","state":"deleted","verification":"unsupported","evidenceRefs":["ev-primary-verified"]})
cases.append(("extra-store", value, "inventory: unexpected stores: shadow-copy"))

value = copy.deepcopy(later)
value["stores"].append(copy.deepcopy(value["stores"][0]))
cases.append(("duplicate-store", value, "stores[7].store: duplicate store"))

value = copy.deepcopy(later)
value["stores"][0]["store"] = []
cases.append(("malformed-store-type", value, "stores[0].store: expected non-empty string"))

value = copy.deepcopy(later)
value["stores"][0]["state"] = {}
cases.append(("malformed-state-type", value, "stores[0].state: expected deleted, scheduled, or retained"))

value = copy.deepcopy(later)
value["signature"]["alg"] = []
cases.append(("malformed-signature-alg-type", value, "signature.alg: expected RSA, ECDSA, or EdDSA"))

value = copy.deepcopy(later)
value["receiptStatus"] = []
cases.append(("malformed-receipt-status-type", value, "receiptStatus: expected pending or complete"))

value = copy.deepcopy(initial)
value["receiptStatus"] = "complete"
value["deletionCompletedAt"] = value["receiptIssuedAt"]
cases.append(("forged-completion", value, "deletionCompletedAt: must be null while stores remain pending"))

value = copy.deepcopy(initial)
value["stores"][4]["until"] = value["receiptIssuedAt"]
cases.append(("stale-scheduled-state", value, "stores[4].until: must be after receiptIssuedAt"))

value = copy.deepcopy(later)
value["stores"][6]["evidenceRefs"] = ["ev-downstream-ack"]
cases.append(("unverified-external-provider", value, "stores[6].evidenceRefs: deleted has contradictory pending evidence"))

for name, record, expected_error in cases:
    output = validate(record, inventory, evidence)
    if output["valid"] or expected_error not in output["errors"]:
        raise AssertionError(name + ": " + json.dumps(output, sort_keys=True))
    print("PASS " + name)

sections.title: Run the lab and compare exact outputs
paragraphs: Place all seven files in one directory. The outputs below are expectations derived from the supplied inputs and validator logic. They are not claims that code was executed while drafting this lesson.

Run `python validator.py initial.json`. Expected exit status: `0`. Exact output: `{"deletionCompletedAt":null,"errors":[],"overallStatus":"pending","pendingStores":["grading-event-logs","nightly-backups","evaluation-dataset","downstream-feedback-processor"],"receiptStatus":"pending","requestHandlingStatus":"complete","valid":true}`.

Run `python validator.py later.json`. Expected exit status: `0`. Exact output: `{"deletionCompletedAt":"2026-10-20T09:30:00Z","errors":[],"overallStatus":"complete","pendingStores":[],"receiptStatus":"complete","requestHandlingStatus":"complete","valid":true}`.

The later completion at 09:30 is valid even though the receipt is issued at 10:00. The required chronology is request at or before verified completion, and verified completion at or before issuance. Every evidence record supporting the completed scope is timestamped no later than 09:30.

Run `python negative_cases.py`. Expected exit status: `0`. Exact output, with one line per case, is:
`PASS empty-stores`
`PASS missing-backup`
`PASS extra-store`
`PASS duplicate-store`
`PASS malformed-store-type`
`PASS malformed-state-type`
`PASS malformed-signature-alg-type`
`PASS malformed-receipt-status-type`
`PASS forged-completion`
`PASS stale-scheduled-state`
`PASS unverified-external-provider`.
sections.callout: Passing the validator means only that the JSON is internally consistent with the supplied inventory and synthetic evidence registry. It is not proof of storage erasure or cryptographic authenticity.

sections.title: Changed-input answer key
paragraphs: Read this section only after running `changed.json`. Run `python validator.py changed.json`. Expected exit status: `1`. Exact output: `{"deletionCompletedAt":"2026-10-20T09:30:00Z","errors":["inventoryComplete: expected boolean","stores[4].until: must be after receiptIssuedAt","stores[4].evidenceRefs: scheduled requires pending scheduling evidence","stores[6].evidenceRefs: expected non-empty string array","stores[6].evidenceRefs: deleted requires verified deletion evidence","deletionCompletedAt: must be null while stores remain pending","receiptStatus: complete requires full inventory coverage, no pending stores, and deletionCompletedAt"],"overallStatus":"invalid","pendingStores":["nightly-backups"],"receiptStatus":"complete","requestHandlingStatus":"complete","valid":false}`.

Trace: the first error rejects a string where a JSON boolean is required. The second rejects a backup schedule dated before receipt issuance. The third rejects the attempt to use verified deletion evidence as pending scheduling evidence after changing the state. The fourth rejects the downstream evidence string because an array is required. The fifth follows because no usable verified deletion evidence remains for that store. The sixth rejects non-null completion while the backup is pending. The seventh rejects the forged overall completion claim.

The retained log is not pending because its legal review is true and `ev-logs-review-verified` resolves to matching verified retention evidence before completion. Adding it to `pendingStores` would be incorrect. The backup is store index 4, while the downstream recipient is store index 6.

Incorrect alternative 1: accepting the backup because 1 October has passed. Time passing triggers re-verification; it is not deletion evidence. Incorrect alternative 2: accepting the old deletion evidence after changing the state to scheduled. Evidence action and state would contradict one another. Incorrect alternative 3: accepting the downstream string because it names a real evidence ID. Strict array typing is part of the receipt contract. Incorrect alternative 4: trusting `receiptStatus: complete`, `inventoryComplete: "true"`, or the signature envelope. These are assertions, not substitutes for correctly typed, independently bound evidence.
sections.callout: Useful failure feedback identifies both malformed inputs and semantic contradictions. The correct repair is to obtain and reference valid evidence, not to weaken the validator.

sections.title: Concrete execution requirements within the 55-minute lesson
paragraphs: Reserve 20 minutes for the original reading, 8 minutes for the completed retention map and scope discussion, 17 minutes for the offline validator and changed-input task, and 10 minutes for review and reflection. Total: 55 minutes.

Learners must run both valid fixtures, explain why request handling can be complete while deletion remains pending, run the independent changed input before reading its key, and run the negative suite. They must submit exact outputs and a traceable decision log connecting each status to inventory and evidence.

The decision log must distinguish known evidence from UNKNOWN boundaries. It must specifically address retained logs, backup key and plaintext limits, evaluation-data lineage, downstream custody, model-training copies, and unlisted stores. It must not convert an unknown provider capability into a guarantee.
sections.callout: This expansion is engineering practice, not additional legal guidance. Apply the provider-neutral evidence protocol regardless of the selected model or infrastructure provider.

activity.title: Write a retention map and a deletion receipt for one AI feature
instructions: Choose one AI feature that processes personal data -- for example, AI-assisted feedback on learner submissions -- and list every store its data reaches, including logs, vector indexes, caches, backups, and evaluation datasets.

For each store, record the retention period and the purpose that justifies it, and cite what drives it: an AI Act log-retention floor (Articles 12, 19, 26(6)), a GDPR principle (Article 5(1)(c) or 5(1)(e)), or 'needs legal review'. Do not decide open legal questions; mark them.

Draft the tier analysis: which AI Act article governs the feature (Article 5, Article 6 with Annex III, Article 50, or none identified), which date in Article 113 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 would apply, and what is left for legal review.

Design a signed deletion receipt for a GDPR Article 17 request against this feature: the fields, a state for every store (deleted, scheduled with a date, or retained with a basis), a verification method per store, and a FIPS 186-5 signature algorithm.
Annotate every receipt field as either 'answers a requirement in text read' (with the article) or 'engineering practice'.

Show an initial receipt while backup deletion is pending and a later status update after verification. Keep receipt issuance separate from deletion completion; explain any retained store and flag an unresolved retention basis for legal review.

Save the seven supplied files and run `python validator.py initial.json` and `python validator.py later.json`. Submit the exact compact JSON outputs and exit statuses, and explain why request handling is complete in both while scoped deletion is pending only in the initial fixture.

Run `python validator.py changed.json` before reading its answer key. Trace each controlled failure to its store index, field type, evidence action, or status rule. Do not count a passed scheduled date as evidence.

Run `python negative_cases.py`. Explain how the independent inventory catches a missing backup even when a receipt declares `inventoryComplete: true`, and how evidence binding rejects unknown, mismatched, pending, or incorrectly typed references.

Submit a scope-limit note covering retained logs, backup key copies, prior plaintext, evaluation lineage, downstream custody, model-training copies, unlisted stores, and the unexecuted signature envelope. Do not claim all physical copies are gone.
evidence: A retention map with columns for store, data held, retention period, purpose, and the governing article or 'legal review'.
A sample signed receipt with each field annotated as obligation or practice, a verification method for every store, and a note of which stores the receipt cannot cover and why.
Two receipt states with distinct issuance and deletion-completion fields, linked backup verification, and retained-store justification; neither marks scheduled work as deleted.
Exact validator outputs and exit statuses for `initial.json`, `later.json`, and `changed.json`, plus the complete `negative_cases.py` PASS output.

A traceable decision log that links every store disposition to the expected inventory and evidence registry, distinguishes request handling from receipt and deletion status, and preserves explicit UNKNOWN and legal-review boundaries.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which store in your map would a regulator, an auditor, or the learner be least able to verify from your receipt alone, and what evidence would close that gap?

questions.prompt: Under Article 113 of the AI Act as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, from when do Chapter III Sections 1-3 apply to systems classified high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III?
choices: 2 August 2026
2 August 2027
2 December 2027
2 August 2028
questions.explanation: The Omnibus set 2 December 2027 for Annex III high-risk systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems under Article 6(1); the general application date of 2 August 2026 is unchanged.

questions.prompt: What does Article 26(6) of the AI Act require of deployers of high-risk systems regarding automatically generated logs under their control?
choices: Delete them after 30 days
Keep them for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, of at least six months, unless Union or national law provides otherwise
Keep them permanently
Publish them to the market surveillance authority monthly
questions.explanation: Article 26(6), like Article 19(1) for providers, sets a six-month minimum and defers to other Union or national law, in particular personal data protection law.

questions.prompt: Which statement about cryptographic deletion receipts is supported by the regulatory texts covered in this module?
choices: GDPR Article 17 requires controllers to issue signed deletion receipts
AI Act Article 12 requires cryptographic proof of deletion
None of them prescribes cryptographic receipts; they require erasure, notification, and demonstrable compliance, and a signed receipt is one engineering way to evidence that
NIST SP 800-88 makes deletion receipts legally mandatory in the EU
questions.explanation: GDPR Articles 5(2), 12(3), 17, and 19 and AI Act Article 4a(1)(e) require erasure and accountability, not a receipt format; SP 800-88 is NIST guidance for media sanitization, not EU law.

questions.prompt: An Annex III system would otherwise qualify for the Article 6(3) derogation. Which characteristic means it is always considered high-risk?
choices: It performs profiling of natural persons
It was trained on more than one dataset
It is offered free of charge
It runs on the provider's own infrastructure
questions.explanation: Article 6(3) states that an Annex III system that performs profiling of natural persons shall always be considered high-risk, whatever the derogation conditions.

questions.prompt: What is the legal status of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework?
choices: Mandatory for all AI providers selling in the United States
Intended for voluntary use
Mandatory only for high-risk systems
A harmonised standard under the EU AI Act
questions.explanation: NIST states the AI RMF is intended for voluntary use; it is an operating model, and NIST notes AI RMF 1.0 is being revised.

questions.prompt: Which item should a deletion receipt NOT contain?
choices: The verification method used for each store
The personal data that was deleted
Stores where deletion is scheduled, with the date
The signature algorithm and key identifier
questions.explanation: A receipt that carries the deleted data defeats its purpose and conflicts with data minimisation; use a keyed or salted reference to the subject instead.

questions.prompt: According to NIST SP 800-88r2, when should cryptographic erase not be trusted without further assurance?
choices: When the media uses AES
When the data or keys have been backed up or escrowed and the organisation lacks high confidence in how the keys were stored and managed
When the media is a self-encrypting drive
When the verification is automated
questions.explanation: SP 800-88r2 says CE should not be trusted on backed-up or escrowed media without high confidence in key storage and management, and that all copies of the target keys must be able to be sanitized.

questions.prompt: A signed receipt lists primary records as deleted and backups as scheduled. What status accurately describes deletion?
choices: Complete because the receipt is signed
Pending until the outstanding deletion is verified; receipt issuance is a separate timestamp
Complete because backup rotation has a date
Unknown only if the signature fails verification
questions.explanation: Signing authenticates a status statement. Scheduled backup deletion is still outstanding work, so deletionCompletedAt remains null until the applicable deletion obligations have been verified.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), Official Journal text
Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI), amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
NIST AI 100-1: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
NIST AI 600-1: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile
NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2: Guidelines for Media Sanitization

cues.text: Begin with a boundary: this is engineering instruction, not legal advice. The classification of a particular learning feature remains a scoped legal review. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 entered into force on the twentieth day after Official Journal publication and generally applies from 2 August 2026. Chapters I and II applied from 2 February 2025. The Digital Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, published on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026, amended Article 113. Its important change here is that Chapter III Sections 1 to 3 apply to Article 6(2), Annex III high-risk systems from 2 December 2027, and to Article 6(1), Annex I systems from 2 August 2028. The new Article 5 points (ba), (bb), (1a), and (1b) apply from 2 December 2026. Articles 102 to 110 apply from 27 July 2026. The earlier 2 August 2025 provisions remain as described in the source text. Use Article 113 as amended, not the unamended 2024 timeline. Sources: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng and https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng.

Show a static before-and-after Article 113 table. Include general application, Chapters I and II, the new Article 5 points, the unchanged 2 August 2025 provisions, Annex III high-risk, Annex I high-risk, and Articles 102 to 110. Highlight the movement of the two high-risk dates.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: A static two-column table lists each provision group -- general application, Chapters I and II, the new Article 5 points, Chapter V and related provisions, Annex III high-risk, Annex I high-risk, Articles 102 to 110 -- with its date under the 2024 text and under the amended text. Reduced-motion mode shows the table without animation.

cues.text: Ask learners which words in Annex III point 3 require legal interpretation before classifying an AI feedback tool. Invite them to distinguish describing a use from making a legal classification.

Check that learners can connect Article 5 with prohibited practices, Article 6(1) with Annex I safety components, Article 6(2) with Annex III uses, and Article 50 with transparency. Remind them that an Annex III system that profiles natural persons is always high-risk under the supplied text, while the Article 6(3) derogation is a documented legal assessment, not an engineering assumption.

Now reconcile two pressures. AI Act Article 12(1) requires high-risk systems to allow automatic event recording over the system lifetime. Article 12(2) identifies purposes including risk identification, post-market monitoring under Article 72, and deployer monitoring under Article 26(5). Articles 19(1) and 26(6) require controlled automatically generated logs to be kept for a period appropriate to purpose, at least six months unless data-protection or other Union or national law provides otherwise. Under the amended dates, those Chapter III duties apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires minimisation and Article 5(1)(e) storage limitation. Article 17 gives a right to erasure on stated grounds, subject to Article 17(3) exceptions. Article 12(3) provides a one-month response period, extendable by two months where necessary, and Article 19 concerns notifying recipients. Article 4a adds a deletion condition for special-category data exceptionally processed for bias correction. The correct design is not ‘keep everything’ or ‘erase everything’. It records purpose, scope, retention, legal basis, review date, and request handling, while leaving classification and conflicts for legal review. Sources: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj/eng and the two AI Act sources.

Display a two-column tension map. On the left show logging, safety monitoring, accountability, and the six-month floor where applicable. On the right show minimisation, storage limitation, erasure, recipient notification, and legal exceptions. Connect both columns to one purpose-bound retention map.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: Provide a two-column text table. Column one lists logging, safety monitoring, accountability, and the applicable six-month floor. Column two lists minimisation, storage limitation, erasure, recipient notification, and legal exceptions. A final row states that both columns inform one purpose-bound retention map, showing the tension and its resolution.

cues.text: Allow three minutes for learners to name one log store, its data fields, its purpose, and the evidence that would justify its proposed retention period. Ask them to mark UNKNOWN rather than filling an unsupported gap.

Ask: if a log is retained, what exactly is retained, for what purpose, until which review date, and under whose decision? Do not accept ‘the law requires it’ without an article and a scoped explanation.

Use NIST as an operating model, not as law. NIST AI RMF 1.0, NIST AI 100-1, was released on 26 January 2023 and is intended for voluntary use. Its four functions are GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE. They are not a mandatory sequence or a checklist. GOVERN is cross-cutting. MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE are applied to a system and its lifecycle. GOVERN 1.1 supports documenting legal and regulatory requirements, GOVERN 1.6 supports an AI inventory, and GOVERN 1.7 supports safe decommissioning. MANAGE 2.4 addresses superseding, disengaging, or deactivating systems whose outcomes are inconsistent with intended use. MANAGE 4.1 includes monitoring, appeals, overrides, incident response, recovery, decommissioning, and change management. NIST AI 600-1, the Generative AI Profile, adds decommissioning questions about retention, security, leakage, and upstream or downstream dependencies, plus deletion tracking for provenance. These practices help organize evidence, but they do not classify a system or guarantee deletion. Sources: https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework, https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf, and https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf.

Show GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE as four connected but non-sequential areas. Place the inventory, retention map, decommissioning checklist, monitoring record, and deletion evidence registry under the functions they support.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: Provide a structured text representation with four connected, non-sequential headings: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE. Under the relevant headings, list the inventory, retention map, decommissioning checklist, monitoring record, and deletion evidence registry. Explicitly state each artifact’s supporting function and that the functions can inform one another.

cues.text: Check that learners say ‘voluntary operating guidance’ rather than ‘mandatory standard’. Ask them to identify which artifact supports inventory, which supports decommissioning, and which supports evidence of a later review.

A deletion receipt is an engineering practice, not a format prescribed by the cited regulations. The texts require actions such as erasure on applicable grounds, communication to recipients, responding to the requester, and demonstrating compliance. They do not require a cryptographic receipt. NIST SP 800-88 Revision 2 describes certificates of sanitization for storage media, including method, technique, tool and version, verification, personnel, date, location, contact information, and signature. Adapting that shape to records is an extrapolation, not a claim that SP 800-88 proves per-record deletion. FIPS 186-5 describes digital signatures that detect unauthorized modification and authenticate the claimed signatory. RSA, ECDSA, and EdDSA are approved techniques in that standard. In this exercise the signature envelope uses EdDSA as an unexecuted illustration. It does not implement signing or verification. A signature authenticates an assertion. It does not establish that the inventory is complete, that the underlying deletion occurred, or that all physical copies are gone. A receipt must use a keyed or salted subject reference, not the deleted personal data itself. Sources: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-88r2.pdf and https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.186-5.pdf.

Show an annotated receipt schema. Color fields that document a cited requirement differently from fields that are engineering practice. Show each store with deleted, scheduled, or retained state, evidence references, verification, and scope.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: Provide an annotated receipt schema in a table. Label each field either “cited requirement” or “engineering practice” instead of using color. For every store, state deleted, scheduled, or retained; include evidence references, verification status, and scope. A short legend explains that the labels distinguish source-backed requirements from implementation choices.

cues.text: Check every learner receipt for a field annotation, a verification method for every store, a subject reference rather than raw data, and an explicit scope limit. Ask what the receipt cannot cover: omitted stores, unknown provider backups, model-training copies, prior plaintext, or evidence outside a recipient attestation.
Guide the retention map, tier analysis, and annotated receipt. Redirect any learner who treats a receipt as a legal requirement or who describes a provider capability as guaranteed.

The worked case uses only the synthetic reference synthetic-subj-042. No personal data, storage system, live deletion, API, provider, or signature implementation is involved. The independently supplied inventory contains seven stores: primary feedback database, response cache, submission vector index, grading event logs, nightly backups, evaluation dataset, and downstream feedback processor. The initial record says request handling is complete because the request was received, scoped, and answered. Its receipt status is pending because four store dispositions are unresolved: logs have pending legal review, backups are scheduled, evaluation data are scheduled, and the downstream recipient has only acknowledged the request. Receipt issuance, request handling, and scoped deletion completion are separate facts. A date passing is not evidence that deletion occurred. The later record verifies the primary store, cache, vector index, backup, evaluation dataset, and downstream recipient, while logs remain retained under a completed, scoped review. Its completion field means completion of the documented request-scoped disposition. It does not mean every physical copy has disappeared. Unknown training copies, omitted stores, prior plaintext, and undisclosed provider backups remain UNKNOWN unless evidence establishes them.

Present the seven-store inventory as a scope boundary. Beside it, show two status cards: initial requestHandlingStatus complete with receiptStatus pending, and later requestHandlingStatus complete with receiptStatus complete and a retained log.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: Provide a seven-row inventory table defining the scope boundary, followed by two chronological status records. The first says requestHandlingStatus is complete and receiptStatus is pending. The later record says both are complete and identifies a retained log. Use timestamps or “initial” and “later” labels to make the transition explicit.

cues.text: Pause for learners to explain aloud why a request can be handled completely while deletion remains pending. Require them to name the four initial pending stores and explain why a signature would not change that status.

Build the completed retention map from supplied engineering-policy inputs, not new legal conclusions. The primary database has a proposed 30-day period after request, for serving feedback and handling requests. The cache has a proposed 24-hour period to reduce duplicate processing. The vector index has a proposed 30-day period for similarity retrieval, with whether a particular embedding is personal data left for legal review. Logs have a proposed six-month period if the relevant duties apply, for safety monitoring, incident review, and accountability, but classification and final basis require review. Backups have a proposed 35-day rotation, while key-copy coverage, escrow, and prior plaintext are UNKNOWN. The evaluation dataset has UNKNOWN retention because provenance and permitted use need review. The downstream processor has UNKNOWN retention and capability until contract and recipient evidence are checked. The initial log record therefore has a scope label and review date but legalReviewComplete false. The later fixture supplies synthetic verified review evidence. Retained records are not described as erased. Inventory completeness is independently compared with expected_inventory.json. A receipt cannot prove its own inventory merely by setting inventoryComplete to true.

Show the seven-row retention map with columns for store, data held, proposed period, purpose, driver or boundary, initial disposition, and review state. Mark legal review and UNKNOWN entries visibly rather than hiding them.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: Provide a seven-row text table with columns for store, data held, proposed period, purpose, driver or boundary, initial disposition, and review state. In the relevant cells, write “legal review required” and “UNKNOWN” literally. Add a note explaining that these markers identify unresolved decisions rather than completed retention conclusions.

cues.text: Check that learners can distinguish a proposed operational period from a legal conclusion. Ask them to identify which row remains physically retained in the later fixture and what evidence changes its review state.

The validator enforces a small contract. States are only deleted, scheduled, and retained. Boolean fields must be JSON booleans, not strings. Timestamps must include a timezone. Deleted requires verified deletion evidence and a verification description. Scheduled requires a future until timestamp relative to receipt issuance, a scheduling description, and matching pending scheduling evidence. Retained requires a basis, narrow scopeLabel, reviewAt after issuance, a legal-review boolean, and matching evidence. Evidence references must resolve in the independent registry and must name the same store and compatible action. A deleted record cannot cite contradictory pending evidence. The request and evidence envelope bind subjectRef and requestReceived. Completion must occur after the request, no later than receipt issuance, and only after all required verified dispositions. completionScope is request-scoped-disposition. The validator does not support an all-physical-copies claim. The freshness comparison uses receiptIssuedAt, not merely requestReceived. Thus a review after the request but before issuance can still be invalid if it is not fresh under the supplied rule. These are consistency controls, not proof that a storage system actually performed an operation.

Display the state machine as three lanes. Deleted points to verified evidence, scheduled points to future date plus pending evidence, and retained points to basis, scope, review date, boolean review result, and matching evidence. Show completion blocked by any pending lane.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: Provide three labeled state descriptions: Deleted requires verified evidence; Scheduled requires a future date and pending evidence; Retained requires basis, scope, review date, a boolean review result, and matching evidence. Add a rule beneath them: overall completion remains blocked while any store has a pending requirement.

cues.text: Ask learners to trace one store from expected inventory, through its evidence reference, to its receipt state. Then ask what breaks if the subject reference or request timestamp changes while the evidence envelope remains unchanged.

Set up the offline lab before running anything. Create a directory containing expected_inventory.json, evidence_registry.json, validator.py, initial.json, later.json, changed.json, and negative_cases.py. The inventory file is a seven-element JSON array and is intentionally independent of every receipt. The evidence registry is synthetic. It binds each evidence identifier to a store, action, status, and verification time, and also binds the subject reference and request time. Explain the registry independently: it is a lookup table for controlled fixtures, not a log from a real system. The validator reads local files through Python's standard library only. It does not contact a database, make a network request, call a model provider, delete data, sign a receipt, verify a signature, inspect backups, or claim that any fixture was executed during drafting. Learners should understand the setup before reading the implementation.

Show the seven filenames and the dependency arrows: both valid and changed receipts use the independent inventory and evidence registry; the negative suite imports the validator and loads all fixtures.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: Provide a numbered list of the seven filenames and a dependency table. State that both valid and changed receipts use the independent inventory and evidence registry. State that the negative test suite imports the validator and loads all fixtures. Use “depends on” text links between each file and its inputs.

cues.text: Ask learners to predict why an empty receipt list, a missing backup, an extra store, or a duplicate store must fail even when inventoryComplete is true.

Read the evidence registry as synthetic test data, not as an execution record. The first three records verify deletion of the primary database, cache, and vector index. The initial records for logs, backups, evaluation data, and the downstream processor are pending. Later records verify the log retention review and deletion of the backup, evaluation dataset, and downstream scope. The timestamps make chronology testable. In particular, later completion is at 09:30 on 20 October, while the later receipt is issued at 10:00. The registry does not prove that those actions happened in a real environment. It only supplies facts against which the validator can check the JSON's internal consistency. If a receipt names an unknown identifier, a different store, an incompatible action, or a pending record for a deleted state, the decision must be invalid.

The Python program is deliberately standard-library and offline. Its useful teaching point is the order of validation, not the Python syntax. It loads JSON, checks root fields and strict types, parses timezone-aware timestamps, prepares the independent inventory and evidence index, then checks each store. It checks duplicate and missing coverage, resolves evidence, enforces state-specific rules, checks completion chronology, and rejects an executed signature because asymmetric verification is not implemented. Valid input exits with status 0. Invalid input exits with status 1 and emits compact deterministic JSON with actionable errors. The program performs validation only. It does not perform deletion or cryptographic signing. When discussing the signature field, say EdDSA is an allowed algorithm label under FIPS 186-5, but the fixture's executed value is false. Valid input exits with status 0. Invalid input exits with status 1 and emits compact deterministic JSON with actionable errors. The program performs validation only. It does not perform deletion or cryptographic signing. When discussing the signature field, say EdDSA is an allowed algorithm label under FIPS 186-5, but the fixture's executed value is false. A passing validator therefore means only that the receipt agrees with the supplied synthetic inventory and evidence registry.

The initial fixture is the first complete worked input. It has the correct subject reference, request time, seven-store coverage, and requestHandlingStatus complete. Its receiptStatus is pending and deletionCompletedAt is null. Three stores have verified deletion evidence. Logs are retained with a narrow scope, a proposed basis, a future review date, and legalReviewComplete false. Backups, evaluation data, and the downstream processor are scheduled or acknowledged, not deleted. The expected output has valid true, overallStatus pending, requestHandlingStatus complete, receiptStatus pending, deletionCompletedAt null, and pendingStores in registry order: grading-event-logs, nightly-backups, evaluation-dataset, downstream-feedback-processor. The expected exit status is 0. This is not a claim of actual execution. It is the exact result learners should compare after running the supplied files.

The later fixture demonstrates a status update rather than a new scope. It retains the same subject reference and request time and continues to cover all seven inventory entries. The logs remain retained, but the synthetic legal review is complete and matching verified evidence is supplied. Backup, evaluation, and downstream records now have verified deletion evidence. deletionCompletedAt is 2026-10-20T09:30:00Z, before receiptIssuedAt at 10:00:00Z and after every relevant request and verification event. The expected output is valid true, overallStatus complete, an empty pendingStores array, requestHandlingStatus complete, receiptStatus complete, and that completion timestamp. The expected exit status is 0. Completion remains scoped. The retained log is physically present, and the fixture does not claim that unknown training copies, prior plaintext, unlisted stores, or provider-controlled copies are gone.

Learners must run changed.json before seeing the key. This is an independent changed-input task, not a request to invent new test data. Compared with later.json, inventoryComplete is the string true instead of a boolean. The backup is changed to scheduled with a date before receipt issuance, but it still references verified deletion evidence rather than pending scheduling evidence. The downstream evidenceRefs value is a string instead of a non-empty array. The receipt still claims complete and keeps a non-null completion time. Trace the failures by field and store index: the boolean type at the root, backup index 4's stale until value, incompatible backup evidence action, downstream index 6's wrong container type, missing verified deletion evidence after that change, completion while a store is pending, and the impossible complete status. The retained log at index 3 is not pending because its legal review is true and its verified retention evidence matches.

Only after the task, compare the exact expected output. The expected exit status is 1. Errors appear in deterministic order: inventoryComplete must be boolean; stores[4].until must be after receipt issuance; stores[4].evidenceRefs must contain pending scheduling evidence; stores[6].evidenceRefs must be a non-empty string array; the downstream deleted state lacks verified deletion evidence; deletionCompletedAt must be null while backup remains pending; and receiptStatus complete requires no pending stores and a completion time. Do not repair this by weakening the validator or by accepting a date that has passed. A passed schedule triggers re-verification, not proof of deletion. Do not accept old deletion evidence after changing the state to scheduled. Do not accept a real identifier inside the wrong JSON type. The exact changed output is an expected fixture result, not a claim that code was executed while this lesson was drafted.

The negative suite contains eleven authored negative cases: empty stores, missing backup, extra store, duplicate store, malformed store type, malformed state type, malformed signature algorithm type, malformed receipt status type, forged completion, stale scheduled state, and an externally controlled store represented as deleted using only pending acknowledgement evidence. Each case must be rejected and must include a meaningful diagnostic. The suite also demonstrates defensive handling of values such as an object where a state string is expected or an array where an algorithm string is expected. The supplied test expectations include 87 independent invalid cases rejected and two offset-equivalence cases passing, but no execution result should be reported unless the learner actually runs the supplied harness. The authored suite's exact expected lines are eleven PASS lines, one for each named case, with exit status 0. Passing means controlled validation against synthetic fixtures. It does not prove real deletion, recipient behavior, backup erasure, or signature authenticity.

Run the two valid commands and record both compact JSON and exit status. For initial.json, expect status 0 and pending stores consisting of logs, backups, evaluation data, and downstream processing. For later.json, expect status 0, no pending stores, and the 09:30 completion time. Then run negative_cases.py and record eleven PASS lines in the supplied order, with status 0. Finally run changed.json before reading its answer key and record status 1 plus the exact invalid output. The lesson must not pretend these commands were run during drafting. Learners should submit their own outputs and a decision log. That log should connect each store to expected inventory, evidence identifier, action, status, verification time, and receipt state. It should separately record request handling, receipt issuance, and deletion completion. It must preserve UNKNOWN for key-copy coverage, prior plaintext, evaluation lineage, downstream custody, training copies, and unlisted stores.

Keep the lesson honest at 55 minutes. Reserve 20 minutes for the original legal and operating-model reading, 8 minutes for the completed retention map and scope discussion, 17 minutes for setup, valid fixture runs, the independent changed-input task, and the negative suite, and 10 minutes for review and reflection. The core teaching is not a promise of a recording or live provider behavior. The practical exercise is synthetic and offline. Learners should submit the retention map, tier analysis, annotated initial and later receipts, exact outputs and exit statuses, the eleven negative PASS lines, and a traceable decision log. They must explain retained logs, backup key and plaintext limits, evaluation-data lineage, downstream custody, model-training copies, omitted stores, and the unexecuted signature envelope. They must also state that the receipt covers only the listed request-scoped disposition. If evidence does not establish a capability, write UNKNOWN. Apply this provider-neutral protocol regardless of which model or infrastructure a real system might use. No provider guarantee is made.

Begin the knowledge check once learners can state the amended high-risk dates, identify the governing article without making an unsupported classification, reconcile logging with minimisation and erasure, explain that NIST is voluntary, and distinguish legal text from receipt engineering.
